patient.chief_complaint: Prolonged altered consciousness, EEG shows bilateral frontal activity, isoniazid exposure discovered after admission — resistant to benzodiazepines
patient.hpi: A 31-year-old White female pharmacy technician was brought to the emergency department after her roommate found her convulsing. EMS reports she was in generalized status epilepticus — continuous tonic-clonic activity for at least 8 minutes before EMS arrived, continuing on arrival. She was given IV lorazepam 4 mg with no response. Another 4 mg lorazepam was given with no response. She was intubated in the field and given IV fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg PE with continued seizure activity (unresponsive). She has no prior history of epilepsy. She has no known medical conditions. Her roommate found no medications in the apartment initially. She is currently on levetiracetam drip started by ED as third-line agent. Seizures have not fully stopped — intermittent clinical movements persist. Critical history discovered AFTER admission (45 minutes in): a colleague at the pharmacy calls and reports the patient had accidentally ingested a large amount of isoniazid (INH) — she was preparing a multi-dose vial and accidentally consumed the powder (approximately 10-15 grams) after a chemical spill incident at work earlier today. The colleague only just learned what had happened. Now the clinical picture suddenly makes sense: BENZODIAZEPINE-RESISTANT SE from isoniazid toxicity.

family_history: Parents healthy. No family history of epilepsy.

eeg.impression: REFRACTORY NCSE on EEG. Benzodiazepine-resistant NCSE in young healthy patient. CRITICAL: Benzodiazepine refractoriness in otherwise healthy young person should trigger consideration of SPECIFIC TOXIN requiring an ANTIDOTE rather than only escalating standard AEDs. Isoniazid toxicity (confirmed from colleague call) is the diagnosis — mechanism: INH depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (active vitamin B6) which is the cofactor for GABA synthesis; GABA depletion causes benzodiazepine-resistant SE. ANTIDOTE: IV pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 5g IV is DEFINITIVE TREATMENT. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: Isoniazid (INH) toxicity mechanism: INH is a structural analog of pyridoxine; it irreversibly inactivates pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6. PLP is the essential cofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) — the enzyme that converts glutamate to GABA. Without PLP, GABA synthesis stops. The CNS becomes GABA-depleted. Benzodiazepines require GABA at the receptor — without GABA, benzodiazepines cannot work. This explains complete benzodiazepine resistance in INH SE.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: PYRIDOXINE (vitamin B6) 5g IV is the specific antidote. Dosing: 1g pyridoxine per gram of INH ingested (estimated). Give as IV infusion over 30-60 minutes. If amount unknown: give 5g empirically. Seizures typically stop within 20-60 minutes of pyridoxine administration. Repeat dose if seizures recur.

interactions.description: Fosphenytoin is INEFFECTIVE for INH-induced SE. Fosphenytoin targets voltage-gated sodium channels — INH SE is GABA-depletion mediated, not sodium channel mediated. Multiple case series confirm fosphenytoin failure in INH SE.
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Do NOT use fosphenytoin for INH SE. It will fail. Use pyridoxine as antidote + benzodiazepines as adjunctive (once GABA restored, benzodiazepines will work).

output.summary: INH SE mechanism: GABA depletion via PLP inhibition → benzodiazepines fail. ANTIDOTE: IV pyridoxine 5g (1g/g INH). Fosphenytoin is also ineffective. Only after pyridoxine restores GABA do benzodiazepines work.

results.title: Isoniazid toxicity and treatment with pyridoxine
results.key_finding: INH SE is benzodiazepine-resistant because INH depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate, preventing GABA synthesis. Pyridoxine is the specific antidote: 1g IV per gram of INH ingested; if amount unknown, give 5g IV empirically. Fosphenytoin is ineffective. After pyridoxine, benzodiazepines become effective once GABA is restored. Prognosis excellent with early pyridoxine administration.

output.summary: INH SE: pyridoxine 5g IV is definitive treatment. Benzodiazepines fail until GABA is restored by pyridoxine. Fosphenytoin ineffective. Poison control consultation mandatory. Outcome excellent with rapid pyridoxine.

key_reasoning_points: INH toxicity mechanism: INH depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP), the cofactor for GAD (glutamic acid decarboxylase); without PLP, GABA synthesis stops; benzodiazepines require GABA at the receptor to work — benzodiazepine resistance = pathognomonic clue for GABA-depletion toxidrome

Benzodiazepine-refractory SE in young healthy patient is the KEY clinical clue — this pattern demands consideration of specific toxic antidote (INH → pyridoxine; organophosphate → atropine + pralidoxime; TCA → sodium bicarbonate)
Standard urine drug screens do NOT detect isoniazid — serum INH level requires reference lab; clinical history + pyridoxine depletion is sufficient to treat empirically

Fosphenytoin fails in INH SE — sodium channel mechanism is irrelevant to GABA-depletion pathophysiology; this is a critical clinical error in the case (fosphenytoin was given and failed, confirming INH etiology)
Pyridoxine dosing: 1g IV per 1g INH ingested (estimated); if amount unknown, 5g IV empirically; seizures stop within 20-60 minutes of adequate pyridoxine
